It is my great pleasure to welcome the distinguished presenters from India, and Lesotho. I thank the minister and her team for cooperating with us and for doing so much to get us to this point and look forward to hearing what she has to say. Please.
Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished guests. We will start our presentation with a short video.

Lesotho, the land of mountains and resilience. In 2024, the kingdom proudly marked 200 years of nationhood, a moment of reflection and unity. And now, in 2025, Lesotho are shaping a future defined by dignity, equality, and progress. From the majestic highlands flows Lesotho's most valuable resource— water, often called the liquid gold. Lesotho continues to face urgent and interconnected development challenges. Nearly half of young people are not in work, school, or training. Gender-based violence remains alarmingly high, with 44% of women affected. The healthcare system struggles with a shortage of health workers, with one doctor serving approximately 17,000 people. Climate-related disasters are intensifying, yet Lesotho's Disaster Risk Financing Strategy remains underfunded. Internal and cross-border migration is also increasing, particularly among young people seeking livelihoods. Fragmented data and poor coordination across sectors hinder timely decision-making. Lesotho responded by bringing the nation together. The government led the 2025 Voluntary National Review Process Through the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning. Even amid global funding constraints and local economic pressures, Lesotho has made meaningful progress. Under-5 mortality has dropped by 25%, from 72 to 54 deaths per 1,000 live births. Skilled birth attendance now stands at 89%, And contraceptive use at 67%. More women are participating in leadership roles. Youth entrepreneurship is on the rise, supported by initiatives like Sebapatswa. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project stands as a flagship infrastructure initiative. To overcome shrinking aid and limited fiscal space, Lesotho is forging innovative partnerships. These include diaspora investors, private sector collaborations, regional trade alignments, and green financing. Lesotho has identified 12 key investment sectors and secured over $460 million to support the implementation of the SDGs. Lesotho's journey towards 2030 is one of courage, commitment, and collective action. From the highlands to the halls of government, Basotho are shaping a future rooted in dignity, resilience, and possibility. The road ahead is challenging, but with unity, innovation, and partnership, Lesotho is not just moving forward, it is rising. Thank you.

Thank you. Once again, Chairman, let me start by saying that the 2025 Vienna was developed through an inclusive participatory approach involving government, civil society, private sector, youth, persons with disabilities, and development partners. Out of the 63 indicators reviewed, Across 6 SDGs, 51% showed progress, 35% stagnated, and 14% regressed. With regard to health and well-being, 54% reduction in maternal mortality has been experienced. And shortage of skills persists, with 89% of women being attended by skilled health workers. We do recognize as a country the need for multidisciplinary teams of health workers to attend to patients, especially in remote areas. And with regard to child mortality, We currently experience 54 deaths per 1,000 children under the age of 5. An alarming 44% of women experience gender-based violence in their lifetime, an embarrassing and barbaric practice that has to stop. To cap this In this trend, a number of legal frameworks for protection and empowerment of women through equal status in marriage and inheritance rights, as well as an anti-domestic violence law, has been enacted to criminalize gender-based violence. We leverage on traditional and faith leaders, local government authorities, to challenge harmful gender norms and promote community accountability. On decent work and economic growth, over 80% of employed population hold informal jobs. Youth unemployment is at an alarming 38%, reflecting low levels of growth and skills mismatches. Innovative approaches to job creation, including establishment of special economic zones to create sustainable and decent jobs through elevated private sector investments while streamlining education policy and curriculum to respond to the needs of the labor market, is being pursued. And in this regard, we have put in place a new Labour Act 2024 that addresses the current challenges, together with an Occupational Health and Safety Act of 2024 to safeguard the interests of the labour and job employees. With regard to climate action, SDG 13, approximately 4,500 people out of 100,000 Thank you. Are affected by disasters. This includes storms, droughts, floods, early frost, extreme temperatures that affect infrastructure and our capacity to produce food. Accessing green climate funding for accelerating climate-smart initiatives remain major challenges. We are enhancing local-level implementation capacity, including systems for monitoring and evaluation, as well as adaptation. Investing in early warning systems, building climate resilience, adaptation in all its forms requires increased funding. Regarding life below water, Lesotho has increased its production of freshwater fish significantly as we continue to maintain the cleanest and freshest water sources by limiting all forms of pollution. Infrastructure limitations in rural areas increases production costs. Best Aquaculture Practices certification gives Lesotho access to premium export markets with regard to freshwater fish. In this regard, we are making progress in scaling up production of freshwater fish and preserving the resources that we have. In terms of water. With SDG 17, we experience significant data gaps in about 43% of indicators because of funding shortages. Statistical reforms under the new National Strategic Development Plan to strengthen statistical systems are in place and limited availability of granular data for analysis and accurate policymaking limit our analysis. We are looking to employ innovative technology for data collection. In conclusion, we reaffirm our commitment to the 2030 Agenda, and we acknowledge the synergies between the SDGs and commit to prioritizing investment in areas where goals are mutually reinforcing. We're making progress despite structural and external shocks, and we call for continued support and strengthened partnerships. I thank you.

Thank you, President, my distinguished colleague from Lesotho, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. India's journey towards Agenda 2030 is not primarily about meeting targets; It is integral to the country's resolve to build a developed India by 2047, what we call Aviksit Bharat. In 2047, India will celebrate 100 years of independence. Like the SDGs themselves, this report is the product of a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, driven by strong political leadership, institutional alignment, and active participation of citizens, youth, civil society, and the private sector. Allow me to share my country's experience through a short video which will be followed by a presentation. Please screen the video.

1.4 billion people, one shared commitment. Bharat ke liye one earth, one family, one future, a commitment. India has accelerated its progress. And the country's Voluntary National Review is proof of its ability to deliver the 2030 Agenda. In the world's fastest-growing major economy, the latest numbers speak for themselves. 248 million people escaped multidimensional poverty. Social protection coverage doubled. 800 million people were guaranteed food security, on track to meet child and maternal mortality targets. Progress has been steady and widespread across states and union territories. India is using data to drive decisions and improve its SDG scorecard, measuring exactly what it has achieved and where the gaps remain through a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach. Technology and innovation are also charting the way forward, both at speed and at scale. Digital public infrastructure, for example, empowers billions of lives every day. From bringing the SDGs center stage during its G20 presidency to bolstering the Global South, India's vision of Viksit Bharat is clear: a sustainable future where no one is left behind.

Could we now move to the presentation? A decade ago, India was counted among the world's Fragile 5 economies and today it ranks among the 5 largest economies in the world. Driven by a profound political commitment to growth through inclusion and inclusion through growth. This transformation is by design. Every initiative is shaped to reach those who need it most, with a focus on well-being, opportunity, inclusion and female empowerment. From household-level improvements to broader social outcomes. The aim throughout is clear: to ensure that no one is left behind. Next slide, please. Transforming lives has been central to India's development model. In just 9 years, as you have seen, 248 million people are estimated to have escaped multidimensional poverty. An achievement rooted in targeted delivery of essential services at scale. Over 500 million people have been brought into the formal financial sector, equivalent to the combined populations of Japan, Germany, the UK, Italy, and Mexico. 150 million households now have access to clean tap water. More than twice the population of South Korea. 550 million people are covered under national health insurance, part of the widening of social protection as acknowledged by the ILO. I do want to note that women have been at the forefront, receiving 68% of all entrepreneurship loans and over 103 million households led by women now cook using clean LPG fuel, which enhances their lives by saving on the collection of firewood and also commensurate health benefits. India has also emerged as the 3rd largest startup ecosystem in the world, underscoring the entrepreneurial energy unleashed across the country. These are not just numbers. They reflect a shift in human well-being. But you may well ask, how has this scale of transformation been achieved? Next slide. India's development model rests, I would argue, on 3 key enablers: digital, data, and delivery. India has invested massively in digital public infrastructure, which is both inclusive and scalable. Over 970 million people are now connected to the internet. Platforms like our universal ID system, Aadhaar, the Unified Payment Interface, UPI, and the DigiLocker to provide access access to government documents have brought technological services to the fingertips of all citizens seamlessly, securely, securely and swiftly. We have strengthened our data architecture to support evidence-based policymaking. From real-time dashboards to high-frequency household surveys, India captures granular and objective data to guide action. And of course, we all know what gets measured is what gets done. Through targeted initiatives like the Aspirational Districts and Aspirational Blocks Programme, we also try to ensure that delivery extends to the last mile. These programmes help to converge efforts across sectors and government schemes to benefit the most underserved communities and individuals. This transformation also reflects India's unwavering commitment to a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach. Our states and Union Territories have been important partners in India's SDG journey. Competing, yes. Collaborating, yes. And learning from one another. But the momentum is not restricted to government alone. The SDGs have brought together civil society organizations, NGOs, academia, think tanks, and the private sector, making progress a shared national mission. And through decentralization, through localization, Over a quarter of a million village councils have been empowered to design and deliver development tailored to local needs. This bottom-up, people-first approach ensures that solutions are grounded in local realities and helps to ensure that no one is left behind. Next slide, please. As India has progressed, it has looked outward, guided by the spirit of its 2023 G20 presidency, the world is one family, or Vasudev Kutumbakam in Sanskrit, we have deepened our development partnerships, particularly with the Global South, and through capacity building, technology sharing, and human-centric innovation, India remains a committed partner to advancing sustainable development globally. India continues to engage actively with the G20 beyond its presidency, underscoring our sustained commitment to global cooperation in sustainable development. Next slide, please. As 2030 approaches, India recognizes that the SDGs are milestones and not the final destination. Already begun looking beyond towards 2047, the year that India celebrates 100 years of independence. Our national vision is bold, to become a developed society by 2047, which is not just about becoming a $30 trillion economy. It is about building a society where prosperity is inclusive, governance is participatory, innovation is purpose-driven, and our cultural and civilizational values continue to guide us. A developed society by 2047, we believe, will mean access to high-quality education and healthcare for all, thriving green and digital economies, strong institutions, and above all empowered citizens, especially women and youth, contributing meaningfully to national and global progress. In sum, India's SDG journey is a story of scale, speed, and inclusion, but above all, it is a story of shared ownership and shared aspirations. And thank you all for allowing us to share the story with you. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Berry. It's a privilege to listen. This quota system, it is enhanced by initiatives offering training in leadership, public speaking, and campaign management for women. Along with voter education campaigns featuring gender components that we put into the framework. With regard to the question coming from Armenia, with regard to climate change, we have made some significant adjustments that ensure that we entrench climate resilience as well as management of our climate in the policies. Urban pilot projects for waste management have been instituted and public awareness has grown through national campaigns. The next question came from Zimbabwe with the production of rainbow trout in Lesotho. Lesotho is known as the water tower of Southern Africa with abundance of water, fresh water. Thank you. Well, firstly, let me thank all those who have put questions for their encouragement and support. By commending our efforts. I won't necessarily take them in the sequence in which they come, and it'll be fairly telegraphic. The Czech Republic— Czechia asked about the role of AI, and what I would say is that with respect to the Agenda 2030, I would really say that diagnosis, data, and delivery are 3 ways in which AI could be mobilized. With delivery, we— you must recognize that overcoming language differences in a country as diverse as India is very important And what AI gives us the possibility to do is literally almost like nano-irrigation, give information and solutions in the local language in agriculture, say. Now, Malaysia asked the question about the multi-level stakeholder coordination system. Rajiv?

Given that discriminatory behavior can manifest in countless and evolving ways, it is not possible to establish an exhaustive list of grounds of discrimination or their intersections. As a result, some individuals may find themselves without adequate protection under one exclusive intersectional framework. This concern reinforces the importance of adopting a cumulative or overlapping approach, which allows for a more inclusive and flexible legal interpretation of multiple discrimination. Moreover, intersectional discrimination may be difficult to prove, and defining clear and consistent legal standards may become more challenging for national legislators judges. By contrast, an additive approach, which considers multiple grounds of discrimination as cumulative rather than interdependent, allows protection systems to better capture and respond to the full range of vulnerabilities. This in turn enables the development of more effective and secure protection mechanisms for individuals who may be exposed to multiple forms of discrimination. Lastly, with regards to the text of the declaration, we wish to recall Hungary's longstanding principled position that migration should not be considered as a primary tool for development policy, and we should refrain from steps that may lead to creating further migratory pull factors. In this vein, we would like to put on record our reservations regarding the unbalanced approach of paragraph 27 of the Declaration and to express that we do not consider it as the appropriate reference point for future intergovernmental negotiations on this subject. I thank you for your attention.
Thank the delegate. Algeria, followed by Belarus and Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. We would like first to commend you for your leadership in presiding over ECOSOC. We would like also to thank Czechia and Saint Vincent and Grenadines for their efforts throughout the negotiation process of the Ministerial Declaration of the HLPF. I would like to reaffirm Algeria's commitment to be to the global efforts of combating and ending all forms of violence against women and girls, promoting gender equality and the empowerment of all women, as demonstrated by the adoption of national strategies aimed at strengthening women's participation and leadership in political, economic, social life, as well as their protection against any form of violence. In order to be clear with regard to our voting at an earlier stage, My delegation would like to express its position regarding paragraphs 61 and 63 of the Declaration. From our national perspective, they are controversial as they do not align with our legislation, culture, values, and do not comply with agreed language in UN resolutions. We believe that ensuring the implementation of the SDGs should be based only on the agreed language contained in the Agenda 2030 per se. However, the controversial language included in paragraphs 61 and 63 do not or does not reflect consensus. Mr. President, although my delegation voted in favor of the overall declaration, we would like to dissociate ourselves from paragraphs 61 and 63 of the declaration and preserve the right to interpret them or any reference mentioned therein in accordance with our national laws. Finally, we would like to emphasize that any initiative should guarantee national ownership and should be consensus-based. Our common endeavor should be guided by constructiveness and mutual understanding. I thank you.
Thank the representative from Algeria. I give the floor now to Belarus, followed by Japan and Saudi Arabia. Thank

you, Mr. President. First of all, allow me to express my gratitude to the permanent representatives of Czechia and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines for their efforts to prepare the draft ministerial declaration and their attempts to achieve compromises and consensus. Belarus voted in favor of the adoption of the declaration, and in light of the inclusion in the final text of a number of concepts and terms that do not correspond to our national priorities, in particular, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and also multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination. Belarus dissociates from that wording in paragraphs 39, 58, and 61. Thank you for your attention. Thank
the delegate from Belarus. Now I'll give the floor to Japan, followed by Saudi Arabia and Senegal. Thank

you, Mr. President. We would like to express our appreciation for the tireless efforts and the leadership of the co-facilitators. First, on the reference to unilateral economic, financial, and trade measures in paragraph 10, we should refrain from using any hostile or controversial language in this declaration with a view to achieving a genuine consensus. Having said that, we'd like to stress that UN member states have a duty to cooperate with other states in the maintenance of international peace and security in full compliance with international law, including the UN Charter, and our measures can serve such purposes. We also share the concerns expressed by some delegations on paragraph 13, which refers to the principle of CBDR. We are convinced that singling out that principle is not adequate here. Mr. President, Japan will continue to focus its efforts to ensure that HLPF will build meaningful momentum towards 2030. Japan stands ready to cooperate with all the member states for a brighter future with no one left behind. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank
the delegate from Japan. Now Saudi Arabia, followed by Senegal, Paraguay, and the UK, and that's the end of the list. Thank

you, Mr. President. First of all, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia would like to congratulate— welcome the adoption of the political declaration of the forum for 2025. We express our appreciation for the efforts of Czechia and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. We support the implementation of the plan of action. However, we express our reservations over concepts that do not enjoy consensus. For example, common response— common but differentiated responsibility. Which may not be in line with national laws and the cultural and religious specifics of states. The same goes for the concept of sexual and gender-based violence in paragraph 63. We confirm our fight against all forms of violence, including violence against women and girls, according to noble Islamic values, national laws which guarantee the protection of and justice for all. The Kingdom supports the national sovereignty of states and underscores the importance of respecting their national regimes and reiterates our efforts to build a more just, sustainable, and inclusive future. We ask that this statement be included in the record. Thank you. I now turn
to Senegal. Paraguay and the United Kingdom. Merci, Monsieur

le Président. Thank you, Mr. President. Senegal aligns itself with the statement by the G77 and China and would like to make the following observations in our national capacity. I would like to express our thanks to the Czech Republic and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines for having conducted the negotiations on the ministerial declaration of the high-level segment of the 2025 session of the Economic and Social Council and the High-Level Political Forum for Sustainable Development. My delegation also took note with satisfaction of the reports of the Secretary-General and the reports of the regional forums to promote sustainable and inclusive solutions for the implementation of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. As we approach 2030, Senegal is aware that it is more necessary than ever to take measures to protect vulnerable groups, to respect commitments on gender equality through the strengthening of social protection systems, which in particular target young people, women, older persons, and persons with disabilities. However, we regret the systematic use of non-consensus terms in this ministerial declaration, which does not facilitate the support of all actors and could could undermine our respective efforts. My delegation thus dissociates from the term multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination and reaffirms its sovereign policy on reproductive health. My delegation would also like to clarify that the concept of gender and all terminology that could be related to it only refer to social relations between men and women. Thank you. of Senegal. Now to Paraguay, followed by the United Kingdom, who will be the last speaker.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. First of all, given the time, Mr. President, I would like to tell you that the Republic of Paraguay disassociates from paragraphs 35 and 45, and we will explain our position on paragraphs 39, 56, 58, 61, 62, 26, and 93. My delegation would like to point out that the reference to other relevant actors at the end of the paragraph does not— is not included in the WHO definition of the One Health approach, and so its inclusion in this paragraph expands the approach of what is currently being discussed at the multilateral level. We are concerned over the scope of the expression. It does not identify or define the sectors or the subjectivity with which one could interpret the term relevant. Ambiguity could give space for non-scientific considerations to be taken into account in the design and implementation of policies. That should be based on science. Therefore, as I said, Paraguay dissociates from that paragraph. On paragraph 45, Paraguay regrets that its wording did not take into account recently agreed language on the importance of food security and open food markets in order to address malnutrition in all its forms. We must not forget the vital role that trade and open markets play in improving food security in all its dimensions and in improving nutrition. Trade and open markets have the potential to support efforts in all 4 of the dimensions of food security, increasing the physical availability of food and reducing its costs and also giving consumers a more varied diet. And for that reason, Paraguay also dissociates from that paragraph.

Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you again to the co-facilitators for their leadership. The United Kingdom welcomes the HLPF Ministerial Declaration, for which we voted in favor. It is a reminder of the urgent need to accelerate progress on the SDGs over the next 5 years. We welcome the focus on this year's declaration on the SDGs 3, 5, 8, 14, and 17. Economic growth and decent jobs are critical to underpinning progress across a range of SDGs. We have heard loud and clear, including through the run-up and at Finance for Development Conference, the need to help foster an enabling environment necessary to attract sustained private sector investment. Building human capital is at the heart of driving growth and development. We must work together to improve global health security, implement the pandemic agreement, invest in UHC and primary healthcare, and tackle AMR. With the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration not far away, HLPA's focus on gender has been very timely. There can be no growth or development without inclusion, which is why the UK continues to put women and girls at the heart of our approach. We welcome the commitment to build on the 3rd UN Ocean Conference to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030, tackle illegal fishing, and end plastic pollution. And we are pleased, pleased this declaration highlights the important agreements reached in Sevilla to mobilize more finance for the SDGs from all sources. So there's much— we welcome this declaration. However, there are 3 points of concern that we have. Firstly, the declaration lacks ambition on climate and gender equality, and we regret the lack of reference to the Paris Agreement and UNFCCC. Secondly, the UK must regretfully disassociate from paragraph 48 due to the reference of unhindered, as we said before. Thirdly, we must disassociate from paragraph 13 given the reference to common but differentiated responsibility.

Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.
